## Animations

Each animation below shows the **tangent-line diagram** for the Newton-Raphson method.
At each iterate $x_n$, a tangent line to $f(x)$ is drawn; its x-intercept gives $x_{n+1} = x_n - \tfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$.
The sequence of tangent lines traces the convergence (or divergence) toward a root.

Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

### Case 1 — Quadratic convergence, $f(x) = 3e^x - 4\cos(x)$, $x_0 = 1.0$

**Behavior:** The function has a single positive root, $x^* \approx 0.2549$ (it also has infinitely many negative roots, outside the plotted window).
Starting at $x_0 = 1.0$ on the convex side of the root, each tangent line lands between the root and the previous iterate, so the iterates decrease monotonically to $x^*$ (1, 0.4798, 0.2857, 0.2556, 0.254850, …); the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step — the quadratic convergence typical of Newton-Raphson near a simple root.

[Julia source](newtonaa.jl)

![Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=3eˣ−4cos(x): rapid, monotone convergence from x₀=1.0 down to the root at x≈0.2549](newtonaa.gif)

### Case 2 — Linear convergence (double root), $f(x) = (1-5x)^2$, $x_0 = 1.0$

**Behavior:** A double root at $x^* = 0.2$. Because $f'(x^*) = 0$, the standard convergence proof breaks down and Newton-Raphson degrades to linear convergence — each step roughly halves the error rather than squaring it.

[Julia source](newtonbb.jl)

![Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=(1−5x)²: slow linear convergence to the double root at x=0.2](newtonbb.gif)

### Case 3 — Convergent near inflection point, $f(x) = \arctan(x)$, $x_0 = 1.35$

**Behavior:** The only root is $x^* = 0$. For $f(x) = \arctan(x)$, Newton-Raphson converges only when $|x_0| < x_c \approx 1.3917$.
Starting at $x_0 = 1.35$ (just inside the convergence radius), the method converges but requires several oscillating steps before settling in.

[Julia source](newtoncc.jl)

![Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=arctan(x): convergent case starting just inside the critical radius at x₀=1.35](newtoncc.gif)

### Case 4 — Cycling (non-convergence), $f(x) = x^3 - x + 3$, $x_0 = 0.0$

**Behavior:** $f$ has one real root, $x^* \approx -1.6717$, where the curve crosses the axis at the left of the window.
Starting at $x_0 = 0$, the iterates are drawn into an attracting 4-cycle ≈ 0.0074 → 3.0005 → 1.9619 → 1.1475 → … and never approach the root — Newton-Raphson can fail even when a root exists.

[Julia source](newtondd.jl)

![Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=x³−x+3: from x₀=0 the iterates settle into a 4-cycle near 0.0074, 3.0005, 1.9619 and 1.1475 and never reach the real root at x≈−1.6717](newtondd.gif)

### Case 5 — Divergence to infinity, $f(x) = xe^{-x}$, $x_0 = 2.0$

**Behavior:** The only root is $x^* = 0$, but $x_0 = 2$ lies beyond the maximum of $f$ at $x = 1$. There $f > 0$ and $f'(x) = (1-x)e^{-x} < 0$, so each tangent line meets the axis to the right: $x_{n+1} = x_n^2/(x_n - 1) > x_n$.
The iterates run off toward $+\infty$ (2, 4, 5.33, 6.56, …, 10.02 after six steps) while $f(x_n) \to 0$ — a small residual does not mean a root is near.

[Julia source](newtonee.jl)

![Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=x·e⁻ˣ: from x₀=2.0 each tangent line meets the axis further right, and the iterates move away from the root at x=0 toward +∞](newtonee.gif)

### Case 6 — Divergent, $f(x) = \arctan(x)$, $x_0 = 1.4$

**Behavior:** Same function as Case 3 but starting at $x_0 = 1.4$ — just outside the critical convergence radius $x_c \approx 1.3917$.
The iterates do not converge to the root; they escape toward larger $|x|$, illustrating the sensitivity of Newton-Raphson to the choice of starting point for flat-tailed functions.

[Julia source](newtonff.jl)

![Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=arctan(x): divergent case starting just outside the critical radius at x₀=1.4](newtonff.gif)
